title: Foundations and Retaining Structures
whyItMatters: Pad foundations, strip footings, ground beams, and retaining walls sit at the boundary between structural engineering and geotechnics. A safe design must satisfy both external geotechnical stability and internal structural strength.
introduction: Shallow vs deep foundation selection, pad foundation sizing and checks (bearing, eccentricity, sliding, overturning, bending, one-way shear, punching shear), and retaining wall earth pressure and stability.
objectives: Select appropriate foundation types (strip, pad, raft, piles, ground beams, underpinning awareness) for given ground and load conditions.
Size a pad foundation for concentric and eccentric loading, including the middle-third rule, sliding, and overturning checks.
Calculate Rankine active (Ka), passive (Kp), and at-rest (K0) lateral earth pressures plus hydrostatic water pressures.
Verify retaining wall global stability (sliding, overturning, bearing) and internal RC stem/base design actions.
learningGate: Size a pad foundation and explain every stability check on a gravity or cantilever retaining wall.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of compressible void formers beneath ground beams in high-plasticity clay.
questions.prompt: When piles and ground beams are constructed in desiccated high-plasticity clay where trees have been removed, why is a compressible void former (or void) installed beneath the ground beams and suspended slab?
questions.assumptions: Consider clay swelling (heave) as moisture returns.
options: It redistributes the peak hogging bending moment into the adjacent midspan zone through rigid-plastic hinge rotation without requiring supplementary lateral-torsional restraint, web stiffeners, or ductile rotation capacity at the support interface

It increases the elastic Euler critical buckling load by halving the effective buckling length between inflection points, provided that the connection detail transfers full axial thrust without slip or local web crippling

questions.explanation: As desiccated clay rehydrates, it swells upward with high pressure; void formers compress at low stress to isolate the suspended structure from heave forces.

questions.prompt: Why must traditional mass concrete underpinning beneath an existing loadbearing brick wall be excavated and cast in short alternating bays (e.g. 1.0 m to 1.2 m wide, with only a small fraction of the wall length open at once)?

questions.learningObjective: Explain when at-rest earth pressure (K0) must be used instead of active pressure (Ka).
questions.prompt: Why must a rigid basement wall propped at ground floor level be designed for at-rest earth pressure (K0 ≈ 1 - sin phi') rather than the lower active earth pressure (Ka)?
questions.assumptions: Consider the horizontal wall movement required to mobilise the active state.
options: Because the maximum principal tensile stress under pure shear equals the uniaxial yield strength according to the Rankine maximum normal stress hypothesis, which governs brittle fracture in unreinforced cast iron and uncracked plain concrete elements rather than ductile structural steel
Mobilising the lower active pressure Ka requires the wall to yield/tilt outward slightly; a stiff propped basement wall cannot move outward sufficiently to let the soil expand into the active state

Because the elastic shear modulus G is related to Young’s modulus E by G = E / [2(1 + ν)], which introduces a Poisson’s ratio reduction factor across the web depth whenever transverse direct stresses are neglected in simple beam theory

Because Eurocode partial safety factors for resistance incorporate a statistical log-normal coefficient of variation for hot-rolled plate thickness tolerances, mill rolling residual stresses, and out-of-straightness bow imperfections across the member length
questions.explanation: Active pressure Ka is a lower-bound limit state requiring outward wall movement (~0.1% to 0.4% of wall height). Unyielding propped walls experience higher at-rest pressures K0.

moduleAssessmentQuestions.prompt: In a cantilever retaining wall with a long rear heel slab supporting heavy backfill above it, which face of the rear heel slab is typically in tension when the upward soil bearing pressure beneath the heel is smaller than the downward weight of the backfill and heel?

The top face of the heel slab, because the heavy overburden soil pushes the heel downward relative to the stem root
